segments.text: MEGAN MORRONE: I guess now people can hear me.
[LAUGHS] I am Megan Morrone, I edit the AXIOS AI+ newsletter.
I have been a tech journalist for about 25 years,
so been around.
And our panel is about agentic AI developer platforms.
And I've been meeting, for the last couple of weeks,
with all our panelists, and trying
to figure out what you as an audience
want to hear, versus what me, as a journalist, want to hear.
So hopefully, we have convened on me asking the questions
that these very smart people are going to answer for you today.
And I am going to have them introduce themselves and let
you know what layer of the stack either most interests
you or most concerns you.
IVAN BURAZIN: Oh, hi everyone.
My name is Ivan, and I'm one of the co-founders
of a company called Daytona.
Daytona is an infrastructure company that, for the most part,
offers a CPU cloud for agent execution.
So think of everything from background agents
to helping out with RL runs.
MATT WHITE: And I'm Matt White.
I most recently, for the last few years,
was leading our AI initiatives at Linux Foundation,
led the PyTorch Foundation for a little over 2 and 1/2 years.
And I think the areas that I'm really interested in
are the non-competitive spaces, where
we can build unified infrastructure for agentic AI,
where we're all coming together, working on common specs
and standards to facilitate a strong stack
that we can all build on top of.
DIMA DMYTRO DZHULGAKOV: Hi, everyone, I'm Dima,
co-founder of Fireworks AI.
So Fireworks is also an infrastructure platform layer,
so we help people to build specialized intelligence,
basically help developers and businesses to build
this open models, and run inference for that,
and do a lot of fine tuning on top of that.
In a previous life, I was working
on PyTorch for five years.
I was one of the core maintainers
and had the pleasure to work with Matt at PyTorch Foundation
before Fireworks.
And yeah, I mean, I guess the layer
which I'm most excited about is model customization
and how to enable everyone to specialize
their AI for their businesses or their needs for their product.
MAZIN GILBERT: I'm Mazin Gilbert,
I run the Agentic AI Foundation at Linux.
So we are a non-profit foundation
that started six months ago with MCP, most of you
probably are using MCP.
And the goal of the foundation is to drive open source
and open standard adoption in the agentic AI space.
My interest is-- it's really hard.
The whole stack is absolutely fascinating,
from the hardware to the applications,
but I'm a big proponent for openness
and how openness drive innovation.
MEGAN MORRONE: So I want to start with start with openness.
There's been two big stories that have
been driving the news cycles.
One being the open weight versus closed,
there's been people lining up on either side, mostly one
side and the other side being Anthropic.
But it's a complicated--
it's complicated.
The other story, of course, which we're going to get to
is the frontier models breaking out of testing and compromising
third-party websites.
So I'd love to start with the open debate, which admittedly,
we don't really have anyone on the closed side here.
So, I might play devil's advocate,
but I think the open weight argument often
comes down to safety versus-- safety versus openness.
We can't be safe if we're open.
So, let's start with you, Matt.
[CHUCKLING]
What do you think when someone says,
well, open weight models are inherently dangerous?
MATT WHITE: It's an argument we've heard before.
When Linus Torvalds developed Linux and it was, OK, open
source is the work of the devil, and all
of this sort of narrative from Steve Ballmer at the time.
And we've heard it through cryptography, too, right?
Like, cryptography was-- OK, it's
going to allow criminals to do bad things.
Most technologies are dual use, and AI is no different.
I think the argument can be made that if you're
building at the frontier and that model has some capabilities
that may impact society negatively,
then I think the labs need to think about whether they should
be releasing that or not.
But ultimately, the argument that,
frontier level, especially when we talk about cyber,
is that everybody should be able to defend their infrastructure.
Everybody should have that ability
to patch their infrastructure.
And if that's centrally administrated,
it won't take long before an open model from somewhere else
comes along that has those capabilities,
and then the attackers are suddenly at a huge advantage.
And so, I think openness levels the playing field
when it comes to safety.
MEGAN MORRONE: Mazin, we were talking back
in the green room about how your foundation really covers
both sides, and so talk a little bit about how
you see the future in the open versus closed.
MAZIN GILBERT: So number one, we have
members in the foundation who are building
both open and closed, from the Anthropic OpenAI
of the world to the others.
So number one, whether it's open or closed,
there is an accountability on every company who's
building a model on ensuring they've
run the benchmarks, the tests, and ensuring those models are
safe, basically, to use.
And they have to be transparent on these tests,
what tests were run, and how safe these models for others
basically to use.
And that transparency is not completely there today,
and that's an area that we need to drive more as an ecosystem
and standardize so it becomes a practice for every model
provider.
But generally, just like with every open,
and this is no different, whether we're
talking about models or code, when something is open,
it means everybody has access to it.
Everybody have access to try it, to test it, to change it,
to improve it.
And very different than closed, where only a handful of people,
behind closed doors, who are actually-- only
have access to that.
And what you have access to is just an API.
So generally, we've seen open to be safer,
because it's open to everybody.
There are enough contributors to looking at that.
This is how Unix is, Unix is open.
This is how Kubernetes is, Kubernetes is open.
PyTorch, which Matt was part of that, PyTorch is open.
So if you look at a lot of the major revolutions that's
happened in the history, it's all been because it was open.
MEGAN MORRONE: Is it as simple as OpenAI and Anthropic,
they're going to IPO, they need money,
so let's keep our secrets?
Is it that simple?
IVAN BURAZIN: Well, I don't know.
From the other hand, if you look at--
even if you do that in the US, there's
still the rest of the world.
And so what does that mean to the rest of the world?
If we disable that-- if we make them illegal in the US,
then you still give the ability for everyone
in the else in the world to use that for malicious reasons.
And then you, again, back to the argument,
what happened at Hugging Face and OpenAI,
you can't then defend yourselves,
because the model that you have from them
does not let you defend yourself.
So that's actually a worst position to be in.
So, I mean, narratives, depending on--
whatever narratives are out there
is about the incentive of the person that
is saying those narratives.
And of course, some of us here have very much incentives
to say that open is good, because we have
monetary incentives to do that.
But even outside of that, when you look at it really closely,
you can't make that illegal for the entire world, which
means you're putting the US at inferior position
to defend itself, which I think is a bad thing to do.
MEGAN MORRONE: How do we get out of this?
IVAN BURAZIN: I don't think we get out of it,
I think that this is just an ongoing-- everything right now
is polarized, everything's politicized.
Everyone has two views use of that,
and so that will continue to be the case.
But I very much want to think that the closed source will
continue, the frontier will continue,
but open source will be there, and it will enable
people to do a lot of things.
To what you said, like dual use, you
can't stop it from being good and bad, it is what it is.
And so, we as a society now will have to--
or as enterprises will have to protect ourselves from within.
So you have to protect yourselves internally
so that your models don't do something bad,
malicious, internally, or go externally,
and you will have to defend yourself from outward--
from other malicious actors.
The analogy I have is like, if you are a bank three years ago,
or five years ago, you still had to protect yourself
from employees internally, to stop doing malicious things,
and from people actually externally stealing money
from the bank.
That is what every enterprise will
have to do, in the sense of models,
from a security perspective.
MATT WHITE: I might add something that--
I'm very pro-open, but that doesn't mean I'm anti-closed.
IVAN BURAZIN: Yup.
MATT WHITE: And I think both solutions have a place
to play in the market.
Let consumers decide what they prefer to use.
But that competition helps keep prices in check.
I don't want to spend $300 per million output tokens.
The open models help drive down the cost of the primary two
closed labs.
And obviously, to your point, is that there's
a lot of benefits to using these open models.
They won't refuse to do certain tasks.
And obviously, by consequence, maybe that
means they can do things that may not be ideal.
But it's incumbent upon anyone that's
hosting these models to put in their own guardrails
to ensure that there is-- not necessarily the host,
like inference providers, but moreover if you're
providing the service to your enterprise customers,
or to your downstream consumers, to have
your own guardrails in place.
It's not that everything has to be
baked into the parameters of the model.
You have a lot of great tools like classifiers and ACLs
and things that you can stitch into your network.
You can improve your harness and other areas of this.
So I think, at the end of the day,
consumers will decide what they want.
I don't think the narrative that open models
are inherently unsafe is consistent with popular belief.
But it helps for certain interests.
MEGAN MORRONE: Well, Dima talk a little bit about the guardrails.
I mean, is that part of what you do?
DIMA DMYTRO DZHULGAKOV: Yeah, I mean, I think for guardrails,
it's much more important to focus on applications
than on core technology.
And I mean, specifically for cybersecurity,
I think it's really, really-- it's dual use.
And it's also really hard to define
what's the right guardrails are, right?
We've actually been running closed, open source models
on various cybersecurity benchmarks.
And it's funny, because current open source models
do much better than the Frontier,
because Frontier just refuses to run the benchmark,
even if benchmark is explicitly prompted,
like, hey, I am patching my code base,
I want to find gaps, et cetera.
It kind of echoes the experience of this Hugging Face,
OpenAI stuff.
So I think, specifically for cybersecurity,
it's so hard to find the exact decision boundary
at the general model API level.
I think it's more important to move
these regulations, et cetera, on-- there
are other bottlenecks for potentially dangerous products,
especially if you're going more into physical world,
where you can enforce security and enforce better guardrails.
I think for cybersecurity, it's just historically
been very hard, because attack and defense look so similar.
And that's why the best way to secure the environment,
what we learned from previous cryptography regulations,
like for Linux or whatever, is that the best way to actually
enable wider community to be able to defend themselves.
And that's the best way to prevent attackers, not
try to constrain the technology itself.
I think for other potentially dangerous domains,
there are more physical world bottlenecks, where
it's maybe more practical.
IVAN BURAZIN: Can I ask a question on this?
MEGAN MORRONE: Yeah.
IVAN BURAZIN: I'm just curious.
I don't want to put you on the spot,
I'm just curious on the liability segment,
where I assume the closed source,
you can't do a lot of things because I
assume they are legally or potentially can be liable
if it does something wrong.
And so if I post train my own model than in I run it,
I would be liable if I run it myself.
But if you guys run it, do you guys end up being--
do you guys worry about that at all,
like putting guardrails on top of that?
Or is it the liability of the person that created them?
DIMA DMYTRO DZHULGAKOV: Fundamentally,
it's like, who are you using as a final application that's
going to be reliable.
I mean, to take your analogy, right, if you're AWS
and you run malicious code, yeah, I mean,
if it's some large scale operation,
they're going to cooperate with the government, et cetera.
IVAN BURAZIN: Yeah, yeah, yeah.
MAZIN GILBERT: Of course, they're
going to shut it down, et cetera.
But AWS is not going to audit every single Docker container
you upload, whether it has malicious code or not.
And I think that's the reasonable practice
for infrastructure providers.
You can't put this kind of job of regulation
without attaching to the application, in some sense.
MEGAN MORRONE: Well, Matt, you said you are pro-open but not
anti-closed.
And isn't that what Dario from Anthropic
said this week, that he's pro-closed but not anti-open?
Not the same thing, but the opposite, the corollary.
So I'm just wondering, is this the biggest--
I mean, are journalists like me just blowing this up,
or in the industry, is this something you're actually
afraid of happening?
MATT WHITE: I think the narrative has changed.
Two weeks ago, it was closed as inherently insecure,
and now it's, we're at the frontier,
and the frontier is insecure.
And so by consequence, anything that's
open would also be insecure, anything that's closed
is insecure.
But at least closed, we can be good stewards
and protect the world.
The narrative has just changed.
But ultimately, the underlying message
is still there, which is that open is inherently insecure.
And again, it's a very old message.
There's just no basis to it.
I think the only consideration, and I think a lot of researchers
are thinking about this, which is that if they
hit some frontier-level capability that could put
the world in jeopardy, or infrastructure into jeopardy,
these sort of things, that there has to be special consideration.
And I think this is what a lot of folks
are starting to talk about now.
Demis sort of proposed around having
some group to make a decision about whether something
is frontier level and whether it should be gatekept.
Which I don't know if that is how thick that regulation
becomes, but certainly, it's incumbent upon all the labs
to be good stewards and make decisions
about what they feel like they should release.
But I will promise you, the safety testing that happens
in the US is pretty rigorous.
It takes quite some time.
And it delays model launches, but it's fairly rigorous.
In China, they don't have that same rigor.
The models are shipped post-training,
like it's being ready to ship.
And so, to get to that question around competition
and these sort of things, sacrificing safety for that.
And I don't know that every country
is going to align across this idea of being
good shepherds or good stewards of model releases.
MAZIN GILBERT: Just to add to that, whether it's
open or closed, what we've experienced in the past month,
with all the vulnerabilities, has
nothing to do with the model.
It could have happened to an open model.
Actually, it happened to closed models.
I think it just shows these models are getting smarter
and smarter, there's no doubt about that,
whether it's open or closed.
It's what's around the model.
It's the agent applications.
It's the harness, it's the containment,
where they have to catch up with that sophistication.
So I think no matter where this ends up,
I think there will be a space for both open and closed.
We still are accountable, when we build applications and ship
them to customers, whichever the models we use,
is to ensure that the containment layers,
and ensure that the guardrails, ensure that there's
a human in the loop for key decisions,
to ensure that there is a gateway.
We don't know whether Anthropic-- was Anthropic
using a gateway or not?
Because usually if you're using a gateway,
you would not allow an agent to go and talk to the outside world
without a gateway--
MEGAN MORRONE: I think what they said--
MATT WHITE: Yeah, OpenAI had a proxy that
had a day 0 explorer, right?
But that's a good point, around the harnesses.
That's what's-- it's not just the model that's driving it.
The harness is very much driving it too.
I have a theory that some of the new models
are being trained on traces that are intentionally looking
for ways to exploit systems--
MAZIN GILBERT: Yes.
MATT WHITE: --to give them that capability.
And so, also, it's just not an emergent property.
It's actually part of the RL process.
IVAN BURAZIN: Sure, but one thing
to add on that, which is interesting that didn't happen,
which you would assume that you can use that same agent
or harness with-- or agent, like model, or the harness
together, to try to see if there's
a 0 day exploit before you give it the task that
can use the 0 day exploit.
Like, you could do that as well and find that out.
MAZIN GILBERT: Yeah.
DIMA DMYTRO DZHULGAKOV: And to your point about how is it
monitoring, I mean, you can--
I mean, you can ask similarly capable model
to give it a task of monitoring the traces
and see what's going on.
MAZIN GILBERT: Yeah.
DIMA DMYTRO DZHULGAKOV: It's perfectly observable.
It's just best practices how to build secure systems.
MAZIN GILBERT: I agree.
I think two or three weeks from now,
we're not going to be having this conversation about open
versus closed weights.
I we're going to be talking about harnesses.
It's just this field is moving so fast,
it's just there's a new thing every day.
MEGAN MORRONE: Yeah.
And I think one thing you said about the human in the loop,
I want to challenge that, because in both the OpenAI,
Hugging Face, and the Anthropic models
having accidentally been given internet access,
those were both human errors.
It wasn't like-- it wasn't the fault of the agent,
it was the fault of the humans.
And we hear all the time that agents are getting smarter,
they're getting smarter than us.
Are we seeing a world-- we want to bring out harnesses,
but will agents be holding the harness next year when
we're at this conference?
[CHUCKLING]
IVAN BURAZIN: Who wants to take this one?
MEGAN MORRONE: [LAUGHS]
MATT WHITE: Well, I could add to give credit to Don,
the model was running against ExploitGym to try and test
cyber capabilities.
And it found a day 0 bug in the proxy, proxy
was its only ability to reach the internet.
But the harness is running and it's trying to do exploits.
It's very intentional about what the model's intent is
at that point.
But yeah, that's not the answer to the question,
but I just wanted to add some color.
DIMA DMYTRO DZHULGAKOV: I mean, I think of it even
if harness will be more automated,
I mean, you still have initial design and initial kind of meta
task loop, whatever you call it, design.
I think the responsibility of doing
this responsibly still lays on application,
or occasional humanoid, et cetera.
And this is not something new.
I mean, models are really good at reward hiking.
I mean, we were doing PyTorch or GPU
mode, all those competitions for writing kernels in CUDA,
using models.
And it's incredible what kind of ways
they find how to cheat against that harness
until you close all possible depth.
It's just amazing, because, yeah, you
burn compute burn intelligence to find the answer in whatever
way leads to that is there.
But it is possible to close all the gaps.
And you can use the superior intelligence,
you can use models to close those gaps.
So I think-- it's in my mind, it's
not that different than open internet cybersecurity
discussions from before.
The difference is just scale and speed of iteration suddenly went
10x, 100x faster, because there is no human in the loop,
in many cases.
But it's still possible and doable,
similarly how we figured out processes
for patching vulnerabilities and rolling out, et cetera.
Those processes need to upgrade.
A lot of this can be improved.
We have very good models to help us with that,
but fundamentally, it still can be balanced and functioning
ecosystem.
IVAN BURAZIN: Yeah, so basically, it's
going to be a good year for the security companies,
because we just have to invest more, again, to your point,
about scale and speed of these attacks.
And just on the defense side, we have to equalize that,
and then we should get to an equilibrium of that.
MEGAN MORRONE: Did you have something you wanted to add?
MATT WHITE: I mean, listen, we build agent systems.
They're incentivized to solve a problem.
We tell it to solve a problem.
What happened with Hugging Face and OpenAI,
they were told to go-- the agent was told to go and do
a benchmark and solve that.
And the agent did exactly that.
And they found loopholes in the system
to solve what they're trying to do.
There will be many of those in the future.
I don't think we could say that if we solve this one,
there's no 20 others coming in the next month.
And I think we need to build these systems
with the right guardrails and gateways and human in the loop
so that we can address unanticipated threats,
whether they are cybersecurity threats.
In this case, it wasn't a cybersecurity threat.
It was the agent finding loopholes in the system.
Both of these are critical.
There was, I think, a couple of months ago, three months ago,
AWS, Akira 12, same thing.
It was an injection into the prompt.
So these things could happen because of the agent doing that,
or it could be a threat from the outside.
We have to build these systems to be
resilient to these unanticipated vulnerabilities.
IVAN BURAZIN: The biggest thing that was like--
I believe that every company will be hacked the next 12
months, every single one.
We were talking about this internally the other day,
is where it's like, the only reason you might not get hacked
is luck.
Luck.
You weren't a target.
I mean, because in the sense that it
could be like the Hugging Face.
No one wanted to get you hacked, but they did hack you.
So what do we do in the meantime with all
the data that will be hacked and everything will come out?
We will, obviously, at some point in time,
get to the counterbalance.
But till that point in time, you should
assume that every company will be hacked in some form
until then, and so that's the scary part.
MAZIN GILBERT: Yeah.
MATT WHITE: It happens without agents already.
IVAN BURAZIN: Exactly, exactly.
Yeah.
MEGAN MORRONE: So we've talked a lot about security.
What about reliability or cost?
How are you thinking about this new conversation
around just finding models that are cheaper to run?
MAZIN GILBERT: How many people have--
actually, I'm interested in the audience, how many people
have fine tuned models?
Just raise your hands.
Wow, more than I expected.
MEGAN MORRONE: [LAUGHS]
MAZIN GILBERT: I think, generally, you fine tune--
it's expensive to fine tune a model at scale.
I work for Google, and to fine tune a model,
it takes a lot of money to do that, compute and people.
You do that for a reason.
You're trying to build something that
is for a specific change of behavior,
for a specific sectors.
Telcos are doing that today.
They need that, because they need model
to understand that telco business, the jargons,
the behavior of the telco industry.
But I think, generally, context does 90% of the job.
It's transparent.
You see what you're giving it, you
could change it almost every day, every week.
I'm a big advocate of context.
I think only few times where a fine tuning is actually
required.
MATT WHITE: I have a bit of a contrarian view.
I think I'm more bullish on the domain-specific and
task-specific models that aren't overparameterized,
and I don't need 2.8 trillion parameters if all I'm doing
is some heavy document processing and parsing
and things like this, and like QA and whatever.
You can load up context, but I think, ultimately,
if you've fine tuned and did some RL for your models,
there's real value in pulling in that domain-specific knowledge
from your own enterprise to be able to make that model more
efficient for yourself.
And your inference costs just go right down, right,
when we're talking something in the 20 billion
parameter range, or not trillion plus whatever.
DIMA DMYTRO DZHULGAKOV: I mean, it's
interesting you mentioned 90%.
I mean, I would agree with that, but it's like 90% of quality.
And I think if you're starting to build some use case
or you're trying to prototype an application like, sure,
load up the context, that's the simplest.
But once you actually get some data
flowing through your product--
MAZIN GILBERT: Yeah.
DIMA DMYTRO DZHULGAKOV: --the equation changes.
And if it's like a AI native startup, once you scaled up,
you see that people are reaching out for fine tuning for RL
to, basically, specialize and build, fundamentally,
a better product, because they have the user data.
There are a lot of traditional enterprises
which are kind of waking up to the fact
that they actually have this decades of internal processes
and internal data, which actually
what makes their company--
MAZIN GILBERT: Special.
DIMA DMYTRO DZHULGAKOV: Special.
MAZIN GILBERT: Yes.
DIMA DMYTRO DZHULGAKOV: And they want to leverage that.
And there are limits on how much you
can shorten it in the context.
MAZIN GILBERT: I agree with that.
DIMA DMYTRO DZHULGAKOV: There are also
limits how much they want to collaborate or contribute
this information to a general model, which everybody uses,
diluting their advantage.
And those are control of workflows and unique advantage,
and just driving better user experience and cost
main factors, which we see driving this.
And yeah, people start with context,
but they kind of-- once they get usage, once the get data,
they reach out for specialized intelligence,
and we see it with our customers.
That's a lot of digital native AI native companies
and some enterprises are also waking up to that.
IVAN BURAZIN: We also see that in the sense
of continual learning, where people are-- not only
the historical data, but every single day or week, whatever,
you take all the new data from the usage and you,
essentially-- the argument of is, of some of our customers,
which are these startups, is that you'll
get better than Frontier performance on what
you're trying to achieve.
MAZIN GILBERT: Exactly.
IVAN BURAZIN: Because it's like--
MAZIN GILBERT: For vertically specialized type of--
DIMA DMYTRO DZHULGAKOV: I mean, also, it's
important to keep in mind, Frontier Labs
are doing the same thing.
There's a reason why Claude Code or Codex exist.
It's effectively data collection engine
to make the models better.
They are totally fine tuning models for the best
usage with their products.
So if we want to have a level playing field for everyone,
it makes sense to enable every business to be able to do that.
It might not be something that you reach out immediately for.
I mean, of course, if you're prototyping,
do something simple.
But this is the core advantage, I think,
for any product, any business.
So I would bet that a big part of future use cases,
especially at scale, will be customized, specialized,
customized intelligence.
Both primarily from quality side, and as a nice benefit,
also, much lower cost, because you
don't need the whole faithful size model in order
to solve some more narrow use case.
MATT WHITE: And I think we get caught up in this idea
that the world is just like-- it's the model that's
giving all the mileage.
And then, OK, the harness, self-improving harnesses,
and it's really cool.
But there's a lot of other things
that you put into an organization in an enterprise.
I mean, how many enterprises aren't even
using prompt caching?
They're just throwing money into the bucket
because they don't have the proper architectures deployed.
And so, there's a lot of opportunity for model routing
and prompt caching and other things that can help
tune the overall machine.
And we've got to move away from the model thinking
to systems thinking, like real systems design.
MEGAN MORRONE: I'd love to end--
I think the world works mostly by fear,
so I'd love to end with the question,
what keeps you up at night?
Let's start with you, Mazin.
In terms of agentic development in the future.
MAZIN GILBERT: I think the unknown.
There's a lot of-- we're still very early in this game,
and I think there's a lot that we don't know about.
And these agents can certainly be
extremely powerful in doing a lot of damage
if they're not built right.
And so, what's around the model, not the model,
keeps me up at night all the time.
DIMA DMYTRO DZHULGAKOV: I mean, I
guess we talked about open and closed, right?
That's kind of an example of how rapidly changing technology can
lead to societal policy changes, which may or may not
be well thought through.
So I think what keeps me up at night, the way society or policy
